claims.text: The liquid-precursor method can produce uniformly synthesized ZrB2 nanopowders with controlled particle size and composition.
Optimized SPS of liquid-precursor-derived ZrB2 nanopowders can produce a dense, single-phase ceramic at 1600–1800 °C.
Improved nanopowder dispersion will prevent or mitigate agglomeration during preparation.
Rapid heating and short dwell times during SPS will limit ZrB2 grain growth.
SPS produces rapid, field-assisted mass transport in ZrB2.
Field-assisted mass transport during SPS enhances densification and produces a finely refined microstructure with reduced pore connectivity.
Pulsed direct current and applied pressure reduce diffusion barriers during SPS.
Pulsed current and pressure promote rapid particle bonding and densification.
SPS can densify ZrB2 at much lower temperatures than conventional sintering above 2300 °C.
The proposed SPS process will yield ZrB2 with near-theoretical density.
The proposed SPS process will yield uniform fine grains and minimal interconnected porosity.
Reduced porosity and pore connectivity will make ZrB2 less prone to hole formation during prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.
The SPS-processed ZrB2 will have greater mechanical strength than conventionally sintered ZrB2.
The SPS-processed ZrB2 will have improved resistance to component failure during prolonged liquid plating bath exposure.
Conventional single-phase ZrB2 requires sintering above 2300 °C.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 typically has coarser grains and higher residual porosity than the proposed SPS material.
Conventionally sintered ZrB2 is especially vulnerable to degradation under prolonged liquid plating conditions.
A 1000-hour accelerated liquid plating bath test can simulate the relevant prolonged industrial service exposure.
Density, porosity, grain size, microstructural uniformity, hardness, flexural strength, and hole formation can be measured to compare the SPS and conventional samples.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in densification, porosity, mechanical resistance, and hole formation relative to the conventional control would falsify the hypothesis.
